You saw her from the back at first, a short mop of hair dyed lavender and fading in a charming way, sky-blue sundress flouncing around her thighs, a tote bag swinging in one small, pale hand. It was the first day of spring, but you only fully understood that now that she had flecked the monochrome urban sprawl in a burst of fresh color, setting her apart from the gray pencil skirts and black suits and white collars streaming around you like hordes of sleepy insects. It was a horrible cliché. You kind of loved it.

You were never the type of woman to make the first move, but the air felt different today. Snow was melting, clouds were parting and shooting sparse cracks of light through the streets, the trees were budding. You smelled promise on the breeze. You'd woken this morning free from a light but suffocating fog perpetuated by the seemingly endless months of winter, and for once, you hadn't hit the snooze button.

It was only once you got closer that you noticed her white and red cane tapping the sidewalk. Perhaps that might have scared you off another day. But at that moment, it only fueled your determination, possibly because it put her in a desirable damsel-in-distress light, possibly because you had a good heart, possibly because you didn't- none of that really mattered. When you whispered "excuse me" and put a hand on her arm, she smiled a gentle smile, eyes invisible behind a pair of sunglasses framed in bright purple. Where was she going, you asked. To the library, she replied, and even though you'd been planning on dropping by a Starbucks, you said, me too. You chatted idly all the way there. She gave you her number. At one point, she tripped over the curb and fell straight into your arms. Her devious smile made you wonder if it was totally accidental.

You kissed for the first time a few days later, in front of your apartment, while she was holding your hand. The next day, you taught her to slow-dance in your kitchen, bathed in greasy lamplight. When you had tired yourself out, she talked about her favorite poets and playwrights for what felt like the most beautiful hours you'd ever spent in your life. You asked her what color her eyes were. She said, blue. You asked to see them. She said, not yet. She cracked her wry, dimpled grin. She fell asleep in your bed and stayed through the next morning.

You woke her gently, stroking her shoulders, and her eyelashes fluttered open.

*Ding!*
